name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q01 - Physico-chemical approach in Reductionist Biology

questiontext.text: Which of the following best describes 'Reductionist Biology'?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Living phenomena can be investigated at the molecular level by applying concepts and techniques from physics and chemistry.

Step 2: Evaluation
In this physico-chemical approach, cell-free systems and tissue analyses for elements and compounds are used to explain physiological processes such as digestion, excretion, memory, defense, and recognition in molecular terms, as well as abnormal processes during diseased conditions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Reductionist Biology is the physico-chemical approach of applying the concepts and techniques of physics and chemistry to understand living organisms in molecular terms.

answer.text: Applying concepts and techniques of physics and chemistry using cell-free systems to understand living organisms in molecular terms
Studying only the external morphology and diversity of organisms without examining cellular organisation
Classifying organisms solely based on their ecological habitats and behavioural adaptations
Observing intact multicellular organs exclusively without performing elemental or compound analysis

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q02 - Contributions of G N Ramachandran

questiontext.text: Which of the following structural biology discoveries was published by G.N. Ramachandran in Nature in 1954?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
G.N. Ramachandran founded the 'Madras school' of conformational analysis of biopolymers and made landmark contributions to protein structure.

Step 2: Evaluation
Influenced by Linus Pauling's models of \(\alpha\)-helix and \(\beta\)-sheet structures, Ramachandran solved and published the triple helical structure of collagen in Nature in 1954, and also analysed allowed protein conformations using the Ramachandran plot.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
G.N. Ramachandran discovered the triple helical structure of collagen.

answer.text: Fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q03 - Cell as fundamental unit of life

questiontext.text: Why is the cell regarded as the fundamental structural and functional unit of all living organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All living organisms are composed of cells, either unicellular or multicellular.

Step 2: Evaluation
Unicellular organisms demonstrate that a complete cell is capable of independent existence and performing all essential functions of life. Anything less than a complete structure of a cell does not ensure independent living.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because anything less than a complete cell cannot ensure independent living and perform essential life functions, the cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of life.

answer.text: Individual organelles can survive and reproduce independently outside a cell
Anything less than a complete structure of a cell does not ensure independent living
All living organisms are strictly unicellular throughout their life cycle
Cells are formed spontaneously from non-living abiotic components

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q04 - Discovery of live cell and nucleus

questiontext.text: Who first saw and described a live cell, and who later discovered the nucleus, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Early microscopic observations laid the foundation for understanding cellular structure.

Step 2: Evaluation
Anton Von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell. Later, in 1831, Robert Brown discovered and described the nucleus as a cell organelle.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Anton Von Leeuwenhoek first saw and described a live cell, and Robert Brown discovered the nucleus.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q05 - Theodore Schwann contributions to cell theory

questiontext.text: Which of the following conclusions was drawn by Theodore Schwann (1839) from his studies on animal and plant tissues?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Theodore Schwann, a British zoologist, studied both animal cells and plant tissues in 1839.

Step 2: Evaluation
Schwann reported that animal cells have a thin outer layer today known as the plasma membrane. Based on his studies of plant tissues, he concluded that the presence of a cell wall is a unique character of plant cells, and proposed that the bodies of animals and plants are composed of cells and products of cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Schwann concluded that the presence of a cell wall is a unique character of plant cells and that animal cells have a thin outer plasma membrane.

answer.text: The presence of a cell wall is a unique character of plant cells, while animal cells have a thin outer plasma membrane
New cells arise exclusively from pre-existing cells through cell division
Both animal and plant cells possess a rigid cell wall as their outermost boundary
Prokaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles similar to eukaryotic cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q06 - Rudolf Virchow and Omnis cellula-e cellula

questiontext.text: The Latin phrase Omnis cellula-e cellula, introduced into cell theory in 1855, signifies that:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The original cell theory of Schleiden and Schwann did not explain how new cells are formed.

Step 2: Evaluation
In 1855, Rudolf Virchow first explained that cells divide and new cells are formed from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e cellula), thereby modifying the hypothesis of Schleiden and Schwann to give cell theory its final shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Omnis cellula-e cellula means that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

answer.text: All living organisms are composed of abiotic chemical aggregates
Every cell contains a membrane-bound nucleus and mitochondria
New cells are formed from pre-existing cells by cell division
Unicellular organisms cannot perform essential functions of life

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q07 - Cytoplasm as main arena of cellular activities

questiontext.text: Which semi-fluid matrix occupies the volume of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells and serves as the main arena of cellular activities?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells require a cellular medium in which chemical reactions occur to maintain the living state.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cytoplasm is the semi-fluid matrix occupying the volume of both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, and it is the main arena of cellular activities in plant and animal cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The semi-fluid matrix is the cytoplasm.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q08 - Non-membrane bound organelles in cells

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs consists exclusively of non-membrane-bound organelles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic cells possess both membrane-bound organelles and non-membrane-bound organelles, whereas prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Ribosomes are non-membrane-bound organelles found in all cells (prokaryotic and eukaryotic). Animal cells contain another non-membrane-bound organelle called the centrosome, which helps in cell division. In contrast, lysosomes, mitochondria, vacuoles, Golgi complex, and microbodies are membrane-bound.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ribosomes and centrosomes are both non-membrane-bound organelles.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q09 - Smallest and largest isolated cells

questiontext.text: The smallest cells measuring only \(0.3\;\mu\text{m}\) in length and the largest isolated single cell are, respectively:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Cells differ greatly in size across different organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mycoplasmas are the smallest cells, measuring only \(0.3\;\mu\text{m}\) in length, whereas the largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The smallest cells are Mycoplasmas and the largest isolated single cell is the egg of an ostrich.

answer.text: Mycoplasmas and the egg of an ostrich
Human red blood cells and nerve cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q10 - Human red blood cell diameter and shape

questiontext.text: What are the typical shape and diameter of human red blood cells, and the shape of white blood cells, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The shape of a cell varies with the function it performs.

Step 2: Evaluation
Human red blood cells are round and biconcave, measuring about \(7.0\;\mu\text{m}\) in diameter. White blood cells are amoeboid in shape.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Human red blood cells are round and biconcave with a diameter of about \(7.0\;\mu\text{m}\), whereas white blood cells are amoeboid.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q11 - Locations of ribosomes within eukaryotic cells

questiontext.text: Within a eukaryotic plant cell, ribosomes are found in which of the following sets of locations?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis and occur both freely and within certain semi-autonomous organelles.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a plant cell, ribosomes are present in the cytoplasm, on the outer surface of the rough endoplasmic reticulum (and outer nuclear membrane), as well as inside the two double-membrane organelles: chloroplasts and mitochondria.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Ribosomes are found in the cytoplasm, on the rough ER, and within chloroplasts and mitochondria.

answer.text: Only in the cytoplasm and inside lysosomes
In the cytoplasm, on rough ER, and within chloroplasts and mitochondria
Exclusively on the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and plasma membrane

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q12 - Examples of prokaryotic organisms

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups represents prokaryotic cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and they are generally smaller and multiply more rapidly than eukaryotic cells.

Step 2: Evaluation
Prokaryotic cells are represented by bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, and PPLO (Pleuro Pneumonia Like Organisms). Protists, fungi, plants, and animals are eukaryotes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bacteria, blue-green algae, mycoplasma, and PPLO represent prokaryotic cells.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q13 - Role of plasmid DNA in bacteria

questiontext.text: In addition to genomic DNA, many bacteria possess small circular DNA outside the genomic DNA called plasmids. Which unique phenotypic character is conferred by plasmid DNA?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In prokaryotes, the genetic material is naked and consists of a single circular chromosome (genomic DNA), often accompanied by smaller extrachromosomal circular DNA molecules called plasmids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plasmid DNA confers certain unique phenotypic characters to bacteria, one of which is resistance to antibiotics. It is also used to monitor bacterial transformation with foreign DNA.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Resistance to antibiotics is a unique phenotypic character conferred by plasmid DNA.

answer.text: Formation of a nuclear envelope around chromatin

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q14 - Three layers of bacterial cell envelope

questiontext.text: Most bacterial cells have a chemically complex cell envelope consisting of a tightly bound three-layered structure. From outside to inside, these three layers are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The bacterial cell envelope consists of three tightly bound layers that act together as a single protective unit.

Step 2: Evaluation
The outermost layer is the glycocalyx, followed by the cell wall, and then the innermost plasma membrane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
From outside to inside, the three layers are glycocalyx, cell wall, and plasma membrane.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q15 - Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria

questiontext.text: The classification of bacteria into Gram positive and Gram negative groups is based on:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bacterial cells vary in the chemical composition and structure of their cell envelopes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bacteria are classified into Gram positive (those that take up the Gram stain) and Gram negative (those that do not) based on differences in their cell envelopes and their response to the staining procedure developed by Gram.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The classification is based on differences in the cell envelopes and the manner in which they respond to the Gram staining procedure.

answer.text: The number and arrangement of flagella on the cell surface
Differences in the cell envelopes and their response to the Gram staining procedure
The presence or absence of 70S ribosomes in the cytoplasm
Whether the genomic DNA is linear or circular

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q16 - Slime layer and capsule in bacteria

questiontext.text: In bacteria, when the outermost glycocalyx is a loose sheath it is called the ________, whereas when it is thick and tough it is called the ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Glycocalyx differs in composition and thickness among different bacterial species.

Step 2: Evaluation
When present as a loose sheath, the glycocalyx is called the slime layer; when it is thick and tough, it is called the capsule.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
A loose sheath is the slime layer, and a thick, tough layer is the capsule.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q17 - Structure and functions of mesosomes

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements about mesosomes in prokaryotic cells is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mesosomes are specialised differentiated forms of the plasma membrane characteristic of prokaryotes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Mesosomes are formed by extensions of the plasma membrane into the cell in the form of vesicles, tubules, and lamellae. They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and distribution to daughter cells, respiration, secretion processes, increasing plasma membrane surface area, and enzymatic content. However, photosynthesis in cyanobacteria is associated with pigment-containing chromatophores, and mesosomes do not form a 9+2 microtubule spindle apparatus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mesosomes do not contain photosynthetic pigments or form a 9+2 microtubule spindle apparatus.

answer.text: They are microtubule-based structures forming a 9+2 spindle apparatus during cell division
They are extensions of the plasma membrane in the form of vesicles, tubules, and lamellae
They help in cell wall formation, DNA replication, and distribution to daughter cells
They assist in respiration, secretion processes, and increasing membrane surface area

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q18 - Chromatophores in cyanobacteria

questiontext.text: In some prokaryotes such as cyanobacteria, membranous extensions into the cytoplasm that contain pigments are called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Certain photosynthetic prokaryotes possess specialised internal membranous extensions of the plasma membrane.

Step 2: Evaluation
In cyanobacteria, these pigment-containing membranous extensions into the cytoplasm are called chromatophores.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The pigment-containing membranous extensions in cyanobacteria are chromatophores.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q19 - Bacterial flagella, pili, and fimbriae

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes bacterial flagella from pili and fimbriae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bacteria possess surface structures with distinct roles in motility versus attachment.

Step 2: Evaluation
Motile bacteria have thin filamentous extensions called flagella, composed of filament (longest portion), hook, and basal body. In contrast, pili (elongated tubular structures made of a special protein) and fimbriae (small bristle-like fibres helping attach bacteria to rocks or host tissues) do not play a role in motility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Flagella are responsible for motility, whereas pili and fimbriae do not play a role in motility.

answer.text: Pili and fimbriae are responsible for bacterial motility, whereas flagella help in attachment
Flagella play a role in motility, whereas pili and fimbriae do not play a role in motility
The basal body is the longest portion of a bacterial flagellum extending outside the cell
Fimbriae are elongated tubular structures, whereas pili are small bristle-like fibres

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q20 - Prokaryotic ribosomes, polysomes, and inclusion bodies

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding prokaryotic ribosomes and inclusion bodies is correct?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Prokaryotes translate mRNA using 70S ribosomes associated with the plasma membrane and store reserve materials as non-membranous inclusion bodies.

Step 2: Evaluation
Prokaryotic ribosomes are about 15 nm by 20 nm and consist of 50S and 30S subunits forming 70S ribosomes. Several ribosomes attach to a single mRNA to form a polyribosome (polysome). Inclusion bodies (phosphate granules, cyanophycean granules, glycogen granules, and gas vacuoles) are not bound by any membrane system and lie free in the cytoplasm.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Prokaryotic inclusion bodies lie free in the cytoplasm without any bounding membrane, and several 70S ribosomes attach to a single mRNA to form a polysome.

answer.text: Inclusion bodies are bound by a single tonoplast membrane inside the cytoplasm
Prokaryotic 70S ribosomes are composed of 60S and 40S subunits
Gas vacuoles are found exclusively in animal cells and fungi
Inclusion bodies lie free in the cytoplasm without a membrane, and several 70S ribosomes on a single mRNA form a polysome

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q21 - Protein and lipid ratio in human erythrocyte

questiontext.text: In human beings, the plasma membrane of the erythrocyte (RBC) consists of approximately:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Biochemical investigations show that the ratio of protein and lipid in cell membranes varies considerably across different cell types.

Step 2: Evaluation
In human beings, the membrane of the erythrocyte has approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The human erythrocyte membrane contains approximately 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipids.

answer.text: 52 per cent protein and 40 per cent lipids
40 per cent protein and 52 per cent lipids
80 per cent protein and 20 per cent lipids
50 per cent protein and 50 per cent carbohydrates

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q22 - Phospholipid bilayer orientation in plasma membrane

questiontext.text: In the plasma membrane, why are the nonpolar tails of saturated hydrocarbons arranged towards the inner part of the phospholipid bilayer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The major lipids of the plasma membrane are phospholipids arranged in a bilayer, along with cholesterol.

Step 2: Evaluation
Phospholipids have hydrophilic polar heads and hydrophobic nonpolar tails. Placing the polar heads towards the outer sides and the hydrophobic tails towards the inner part ensures that the nonpolar tails of saturated hydrocarbons are protected from the aqueous environment.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This orientation protects the nonpolar hydrophobic tails from the aqueous environment.

answer.text: To allow free passage of polar ions through the core by simple diffusion
To bind peripheral proteins covalently to the interior of the bilayer
To ensure that the hydrophobic nonpolar tails are protected from the aqueous environment
To prevent lateral movement of integral proteins within the lipid bilayer

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q23 - Fluid mosaic model by Singer and Nicolson

questiontext.text: According to the fluid mosaic model proposed by Singer and Nicolson (1972), what enables the lateral movement of proteins within the overall lipid bilayer?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The fluid mosaic model describes the dynamic structural organisation of biological membranes.

Step 2: Evaluation
According to Singer and Nicolson (1972), the quasi-fluid nature of lipid enables lateral movement of proteins within the overall bilayer, and this ability to move within the membrane is measured as its fluidity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The quasi-fluid nature of the lipid bilayer enables lateral movement of proteins.

answer.text: Calcium pectate bridges in the middle lamella

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q24 - Functions dependent on plasma membrane fluidity

questiontext.text: The fluid nature of the plasma membrane is important for which of the following cellular processes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Membrane fluidity is essential for dynamic cellular events that require membrane remodelling and protein mobility.

Step 2: Evaluation
The fluid nature of the membrane is important for functions such as cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, and cell division. In contrast, rigid mechanical protection against bursting is a function of the cell wall, and rRNA synthesis occurs in the nucleolus.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, and cell division depend on membrane fluidity.

answer.text: Providing rigid structural support to prevent bacterial bursting
Cell growth, formation of intercellular junctions, secretion, endocytosis, and cell division

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q25 - Passive transport, osmosis, and carrier proteins

questiontext.text: How do neutral solutes, water, and polar molecules respectively move across the plasma membrane along their concentration gradient without energy expenditure?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Passive transport moves molecules across the selectively permeable plasma membrane along the concentration gradient (higher to lower concentration) without ATP.

Step 2: Evaluation
Neutral solutes move across the membrane by simple diffusion. Water moves across the membrane from higher to lower concentration by osmosis. Polar molecules cannot pass through the nonpolar lipid bilayer directly and therefore require a carrier protein of the membrane to facilitate their transport.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Neutral solutes move by simple diffusion, water moves by osmosis, and polar molecules move via carrier proteins.

answer.text: Simple diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated transport via carrier proteins
Facilitated transport, active transport, and simple diffusion

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q26 - Active transport across plasma membrane

questiontext.text: Which of the following is an example of active transport across the plasma membrane in which ATP is utilised?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Active transport moves ions or molecules across the membrane against their concentration gradient (from lower to higher concentration) and requires energy in the form of ATP.

Step 2: Evaluation
The \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) pump is a classic example of active transport. Simple diffusion of neutral solutes and osmosis of water are passive processes that do not consume ATP.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) pump is an energy-dependent active transport process.

answer.text: Simple diffusion of neutral solutes down a concentration gradient
Movement of water by osmosis from higher to lower concentration
Transport of ions by the \(\text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+\) pump against their concentration gradient
Passive movement of gases across the phospholipid bilayer

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q27 - Cell wall composition in algae and plants

questiontext.text: How does the chemical composition of the algal cell wall differ from that of other plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cell wall is a non-living rigid outer covering of the plasma membrane in fungi and plants, whose chemical composition varies between algae and other plants.

Step 2: Evaluation
Algae have a cell wall made of cellulose, galactans, mannans, and minerals like calcium carbonate. In other plants, the cell wall consists of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and proteins.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Algal cell walls contain cellulose, galactans, mannans, and minerals like calcium carbonate, whereas other plants have cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and proteins.

answer.text: Algal cell walls contain only peptidoglycan, whereas plant cell walls contain chitin
Algal cell walls are made of cellulose, galactans, mannans, and calcium carbonate, whereas other plant cell walls consist of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins, and proteins
Algal cell walls lack cellulose completely and are composed solely of calcium pectate
Other plant cell walls contain galactans and mannans, whereas algal cell walls contain pectins and hemicellulose

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q28 - Primary and secondary cell wall formation

questiontext.text: In a maturing plant cell, where is the secondary cell wall formed relative to the primary cell wall and the plasma membrane?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cell wall of a young plant cell is the primary wall, which is capable of growth.

Step 2: Evaluation
As the plant cell matures, the growth capability of the primary wall gradually diminishes, and the secondary wall is formed on the inner side of the cell, i.e., towards the plasma membrane (between the primary wall and the plasma membrane).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The secondary wall is formed on the inner side of the primary wall, towards the plasma membrane.

answer.text: On the outer side of the middle lamella, away from the plasma membrane
Between the middle lamella and the primary cell wall
Inside the tonoplast of the central vacuole
On the inner side of the primary wall, towards the plasma membrane

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q29 - Middle lamella and plasmodesmata

questiontext.text: The middle lamella that holds neighbouring plant cells together is mainly composed of ________, and the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells is connected by ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Adjacent plant cells are cemented together and communicate cytoplasmically across their cell walls.

Step 2: Evaluation
The middle lamella is a layer mainly made of calcium pectate that glues neighbouring cells together. Both the cell wall and middle lamellae may be traversed by plasmodesmata, which connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The middle lamella is mainly composed of calcium pectate, and neighbouring cytoplasms are connected by plasmodesmata.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q30 - Components of the endomembrane system

questiontext.text: Which group of organelles is excluded from the endomembrane system because their functions are not coordinated with the ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes, and vacuoles?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The endomembrane system groups membranous organelles whose functions are coordinated: the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), Golgi complex, lysosomes, and vacuoles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because the functions of mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes are not coordinated with those four components, they are not considered part of the endomembrane system.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Mitochondria, chloroplasts, and peroxisomes are excluded from the endomembrane system.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q31 - Intracellular compartments and ER types

questiontext.text: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) divides the intracellular space into two distinct compartments, namely:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The endoplasmic reticulum forms a network of tiny tubular structures scattered in the cytoplasm.

Step 2: Evaluation
By forming a continuous membranous network, the ER divides the intracellular space into the luminal compartment (inside the ER) and the extra-luminal compartment (the cytoplasm).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The two compartments are the luminal and extra-luminal compartments.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q32 - Golgi apparatus cisternae and synthesis

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Golgi apparatus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The Golgi apparatus consists of stacked flat, disc-shaped sacs or cisternae (0.5 to 1.0 \(\mu\text{m}\) diameter) concentrically arranged near the nucleus.

Step 2: Evaluation
The Golgi cisternae have a distinct convex cis (forming) face and a concave trans (maturing) face that are entirely different yet interconnected. It packages materials from the ER and is the important site for the formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The Golgi apparatus is the important site for the formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids, with interconnected cis and trans faces.

answer.text: Its cisternae measure 5 to 10 \(\mu\text{m}\) in diameter and are found only in prokaryotes
Its concave cis face receives vesicles from the plasma membrane for excretion
It is the primary site for synthesis of steroidal hormones and aerobic ATP
It has interconnected convex cis and concave trans faces and is an important site of glycoprotein and glycolipid formation

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q33 - Lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes and pH

questiontext.text: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicular structures formed by packaging in the Golgi apparatus. Their hydrolytic enzymes are optimally active at:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes (hydrolases such as lipases, proteases, and carbohydrases) capable of digesting carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.

Step 2: Evaluation
Isolated lysosomal vesicles are rich in these hydrolases, which are optimally active at acidic pH.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes are optimally active at acidic pH.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q34 - Vacuole volume and tonoplast in plants

questiontext.text: In plant cells, vacuoles bound by a single membrane called the tonoplast can occupy up to what percentage of the cell volume?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The vacuole is a membrane-bound space in the cytoplasm containing water, sap, excretory products, and other non-useful materials.

Step 2: Evaluation
In plant cells, vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the volume of the cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plant vacuoles can occupy up to 90 per cent of the cell volume.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q35 - Contractile vacuole in Amoeba

questiontext.text: In Amoeba, which structure is important for osmoregulation and excretion?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different types of vacuoles perform specialised functions in protists and unicellular organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Amoeba, the contractile vacuole is important for osmoregulation and excretion, whereas food vacuoles in protists are formed by engulfing food particles.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The contractile vacuole is responsible for osmoregulation and excretion in Amoeba.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q36 - Dimensions and division of mitochondria

questiontext.text: Typically, a sausage-shaped or cylindrical mitochondrion has a diameter of ________ and a length of ________, and divides by ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Mitochondria vary in number per cell depending on physiological activity, as well as in shape and size.

Step 2: Evaluation
Typically, a mitochondrion is sausage-shaped or cylindrical with a diameter of \(0.2\text{--}1.0\;\mu\text{m}\) (average \(0.5\;\mu\text{m}\)) and length \(1.0\text{--}4.1\;\mu\text{m}\), and it divides by fission.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The typical diameter is \(0.2\text{--}1.0\;\mu\text{m}\), length is \(1.0\text{--}4.1\;\mu\text{m}\), and division occurs by fission.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q37 - Mitochondrial matrix contents and cristae

questiontext.text: Which of the following sets of components is present inside the mitochondrial matrix?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Each mitochondrion has an outer membrane and an inner membrane dividing its lumen into an outer compartment and an inner compartment filled with a dense homogeneous matrix.

Step 2: Evaluation
The mitochondrial matrix possesses a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes, and the components required for protein synthesis. It does not contain 80S ribosomes, linear histone-bound chromosomes, or chlorophyll.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The mitochondrial matrix contains a single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes, and components for protein synthesis.

answer.text: Single circular DNA molecule, a few RNA molecules, 70S ribosomes, and protein synthesis components
Hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH and calcium pectate

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q38 - Occurrence and types of plastids

questiontext.text: Plastids are found in all plant cells and in ________, and chromoplasts contain fat-soluble ________ pigments such as carotene and xanthophylls.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Plastids are large pigment-containing or nutrient-storing organelles easily observed under the microscope.

Step 2: Evaluation
Plastids are found in all plant cells and in euglenoides. Based on pigments, they are classified into chloroplasts, chromoplasts, and leucoplasts. Chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments like carotene and xanthophylls, giving yellow, orange, or red colour to plant parts.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plastids occur in all plant cells and euglenoides, and chromoplasts contain fat-soluble carotenoid pigments.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q39 - Number and dimensions of chloroplasts

questiontext.text: How many chloroplasts are present per cell in Chlamydomonas versus a leaf mesophyll cell, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The number of chloroplasts per cell varies depending on the organism and cell type.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Chlamydomonas, a green alga, there is 1 chloroplast per cell, whereas in the mesophyll cells of leaves there are 20–40 chloroplasts per cell.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chlamydomonas has 1 chloroplast per cell and mesophyll cells have 20–40 chloroplasts per cell.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q40 - Internal structure and membranes of chloroplast

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements regarding the internal organisation of a chloroplast is incorrect?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chloroplasts are double-membrane-bound organelles containing an internal stroma and a thylakoid membrane system.

Step 2: Evaluation
Of the two membranes, the inner chloroplast membrane is relatively less permeable. Thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana and connected across different grana by flat membranous tubules called stroma lamellae. Chlorophyll pigments are present in the thylakoids. The stroma contains small double-stranded circular DNA molecules and 70S ribosomes (which are smaller than the 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, not larger).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Chloroplast ribosomes are 70S, which are smaller—not larger—than 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes.

answer.text: The inner chloroplast membrane is relatively less permeable than the outer membrane
Flat membranous tubules called stroma lamellae connect the thylakoids of different grana
The stroma contains small, double-stranded circular DNA molecules and enzymes for carbohydrate synthesis
The ribosomes of the chloroplast stroma are 80S and larger than cytoplasmic ribosomes

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q41 - Sites of light and dark reactions in chloroplast

questiontext.text: In plant chloroplasts, the light reactions and dark reactions of photosynthesis take place respectively in the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Chloroplasts trap light energy and synthesise carbohydrates through two spatially separated sets of reactions.

Step 2: Evaluation
The grana (stacks of thylakoids containing chlorophyll) are the site of light reactions, while the stroma (containing carbohydrate-synthesising enzymes) is the site of dark reactions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Light reactions occur in the grana, and dark reactions occur in the stroma.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q42 - Svedberg unit and ribosome subunits

questiontext.text: In 70S and 80S ribosomes, what does 'S' (Svedberg's Unit) stand for, and what is it an indirect measure of?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ribosomes are composed of ribonucleic acid (RNA) and proteins and consist of a larger and a smaller subunit.

Step 2: Evaluation
In 70S (50S + 30S) and 80S (60S + 40S) ribosomes, 'S' (Svedberg's Unit) stands for the sedimentation coefficient, which is indirectly a measure of density and size.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
'S' stands for the sedimentation coefficient and is an indirect measure of density and size.

answer.text: Solvent affinity; indirect measure of lipid content
Surface area; indirect measure of enzymatic rate
Sedimentation coefficient; indirect measure of density and size
Structural stability; indirect measure of membrane thickness

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q43 - Composition and functions of cytoskeleton

questiontext.text: An elaborate network of filamentous proteinaceous structures present in the cytoplasm, collectively called the cytoskeleton, consists of:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cytoskeleton is involved in mechanical support, motility, and maintenance of cell shape.

Step 2: Evaluation
It consists of three types of filamentous proteinaceous structures: microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The cytoskeleton is composed of microtubules, microfilaments, and intermediate filaments.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q44 - Ultrastructure of eukaryotic cilia and flagella

questiontext.text: In the axoneme of a eukaryotic cilium or flagellum, how many radial spokes are present, and from what structure do both cilia and flagella emerge?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The axoneme of eukaryotic cilia and flagella exhibits a 9+2 microtubule array covered by the plasma membrane.

Step 2: Evaluation
The central pair of tubules is connected by bridges and enclosed by a central sheath, which is connected to one tubule of each of the nine peripheral doublets by a radial spoke—making 9 radial spokes in total. Both cilia and flagella emerge from centriole-like structures called basal bodies.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
There are 9 radial spokes, and both cilia and flagella emerge from basal bodies.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q45 - Centriole cartwheel organisation and functions

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the centrosome and centrioles in animal cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A centrosome usually contains two cylindrical centrioles surrounded by amorphous pericentriolar materials, lying perpendicular to each other.

Step 2: Evaluation
Each centriole has a cartwheel-like organisation made of nine evenly spaced peripheral fibrils of tubulin protein, where each peripheral fibril is a triplet. The central proteinaceous hub in the proximal region is connected to the peripheral triplets by proteinaceous radial spokes. Centrioles form the basal body of cilia or flagella and spindle fibres that give rise to the spindle apparatus during cell division in animal cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Centrioles lie perpendicular to each other, have nine peripheral tubulin triplets connected to a central hub, and form basal bodies and spindle apparatus.

answer.text: Two centrioles lie perpendicular to each other, each having nine peripheral tubulin triplets connected to a central proteinaceous hub
Centrioles are membrane-bound organelles containing 70S ribosomes and circular DNA
Each peripheral fibril of a centriole is a doublet arranged around a central pair of microtubules
Centrioles are present in all higher plant cells and absent in animal cells

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q46 - Nuclear envelope, perinuclear space, and enucleate cells

questiontext.text: Which of the following is correct regarding the nuclear envelope and the presence of a nucleus in mature eukaryotic cells?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nuclear envelope consists of two parallel membranes separated by a perinuclear space of 10 to 50 nm, interrupted by nuclear pores.

Step 2: Evaluation
The outer nuclear membrane usually remains continuous with the endoplasmic reticulum and bears ribosomes on it. While most eukaryotic cells have one nucleus, some mature cells lack a nucleus—specifically erythrocytes of many mammals and sieve tube cells of vascular plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes, and mature mammalian erythrocytes and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus.

answer.text: The perinuclear space is 5–10 \(\mu\text{m}\) wide and prevents all movement of RNA
The inner nuclear membrane is continuous with the smooth endoplasmic reticulum
The outer nuclear membrane is continuous with the ER and bears ribosomes, while mature mammalian erythrocytes and sieve tube cells lack a nucleus
The nucleolus is enclosed by a single membrane called the tonoplast

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q47 - Chromatin composition and human DNA length

questiontext.text: Who gave the name 'chromatin' to the nuclear material stained by basic dyes, and approximately how long is the DNA thread distributed among the 46 chromosomes of a single human cell?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Interphase chromatin contains DNA, basic proteins called histones, non-histone proteins, and RNA.

Step 2: Evaluation
The material of the nucleus stained by basic dyes was given the name chromatin by Flemming. A single human cell has an approximately two metre long thread of DNA distributed among its 46 (23 pairs) chromosomes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Flemming named chromatin, and a single human cell contains approximately two metres of DNA.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELLTHEUNITOFLIFE_MCQ_Q48 - Kinetochores and microbodies in eukaryotic cells

questiontext.text: Disc-shaped structures present on the sides of the centromere are called ________, and membrane-bound minute vesicles containing various enzymes in both plant and animal cells are called ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Eukaryotic chromosomes possess specialised centromeric structures during cell division, while eukaryotic cytoplasm also contains small enzyme-filled vesicles.

Step 2: Evaluation
Every chromosome has a primary constriction (centromere) on the sides of which disc-shaped structures called kinetochores are present. Microbodies are membrane-bound minute vesicles containing various enzymes present in both plant and animal cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The disc-shaped structures on the sides of the centromere are kinetochores, and the enzyme-containing minute vesicles are microbodies.
